analysis.one_liner: Ends fixed federal farm subsidy checks paid regardless of crop prices or need.
analysis.headline: The bill to end roughly $5 billion a year in automatic farm payments never got a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal 'direct payments' go to certain farm operators every year based on old acreage and yield history — not on current prices, losses, or whether the person even farms. This bill would have shut the program off starting with the 2013 crop year, saving the government nearly $5 billion annually. The bill was sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would save nearly $5 billion a year under a program the bill's findings show goes largely to the largest farm operations — payments are concentrated, with more than 51 percent flowing to just 10 percent of recipients, and some paid to people who do not farm at all.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and small farms not receiving payments

how_it_helps.text: Direct payments cost the federal government nearly $5 billion annually and are fixed payments with no connection to market conditions or producers' actual losses.
Payments are set by historical acreage and yield and are payable even to people who do not farm and to producers who do not grow the covered commodity.

Payments go to producers on fewer than 22 percent of all farms, with more than 51 percent flowing to 10 percent of recipients and 73 percent to 25 percent — concentrated on the largest operations least likely to need support.
The termination applied beginning with the 2013 crop year, repealing the direct-payment sections of the 2008 farm law immediately rather than waiting for a new farm bill.

analysis.who_pays: The roughly 10 percent of farm operations that receive direct payments would lose the guaranteed checks — a group the bill's own findings show is dominated by the largest farms, during a period when net farm income was projected at $112 billion, the second-highest on record.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large farm operations receiving direct payments

drawbacks.text: Direct payments, whatever their flaws, give farm operators a predictable income floor; cutting them without any replacement removes a guaranteed cushion when a farm's revenue collapses, which is the argument for the income-insurance alternatives Congress later debated.
The cuts would fall on the whole class of payment recipients at once beginning with the 2013 crop year, including some smaller producers among them, rather than being phased down.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings are broad and the cost narrow: nearly $5 billion a year in mandatory spending ends, borne by a group receiving payments regardless of need during near-record farm income. The real objection is fairness to the minority of recipients who do rely on the checks in bad years — but the bill's design, an immediate clean repeal, was the version most favorable to taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator Claire McCaskill introduced the bill on February 14, 2013, joined by Republican Senator Jeff Flake, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

The bill's findings noted the Senate had already passed a farm bill (S. 3240, 112th Congress) in June 2012 that eliminated direct payments, and the House Agriculture Committee had reported a companion bill, showing prior bipartisan action on the same change.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — and the bill died at the end of the 113th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The farm operations that receive direct payments — a group dominated by the largest producers — continued collecting roughly $5 billion a year in fixed payments for the rest of the 113th Congress because the committee never acted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large farms that kept the payments

for.name: Sen. Claire McCaskill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to terminate direct payments beginning with the 2013 crop year.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Flake
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor, making the bill bipartisan.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or report — leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and a Republican cosponsor, and its findings cite a 2012 Senate-passed farm bill that had already voted to eliminate direct payments; no party-division votes ever occurred because the committee never acted.

industries.industry: Large farm operations receiving direct payments
industries.note: The bill would have ended their guaranteed annual checks — more than half of all payment dollars flow to the top 10 percent of recipients. Keeping the payments intact preserves a fixed subsidy that runs against taxpayers' interest.

industries.industry: Producers of covered commodities (corn, wheat, rice, cotton and other program crops)
industries.note: Direct-payment recipients growing these crops would lose the checks, while producers who do not grow covered commodities already get nothing from the program. The payments are unconnected to current prices or losses, so the bill's repeal would not have changed market returns.
